transcript:
So, with exams coming up, I want to talk about something your parents have probably told you a hundred times. Get a good night's sleep, because it helps you remember what you studied. Lots of people believe this, and as far as scientists can tell, it's actually true. The more interesting question is why it's true, and there are two competing explanations.

The first explanation is fairly simple. While you're awake, new things keep coming into your head. Conversations, messages, songs, whatever. Each new thing can push against the memories you made earlier and make them harder to find. Psychologists call this interference. When you're asleep, almost nothing new comes in. So, on this view, sleep doesn't do anything special. It just gives your memories a quiet place to sit, like a sign on a door that says do not disturb.

The second explanation says sleep is much more active than that. While you sleep, the brain goes back over what you learned during the day and makes those memories stronger. This is called consolidation. So sleep isn't just a quiet room. It's more like a night shift, when workers come in and fix up the day's work.

Now, how could we tell these two apart? Here's the interesting part. Researchers have recorded brain cells in rats while the rats ran through a maze. Certain cells fired in a particular order as a rat moved along the path. Later, when the rat was asleep, those same cells fired again, in roughly the same order, and often faster. It looked as if the sleeping brain was running through the maze again. A quiet room doesn't do that.

An even clearer test was done with people. Volunteers learned where about fifty pictures appeared on a computer screen, and each picture came with its own sound. A cat picture came with a meow, for example. Then they took a nap. While they were in deep sleep, the researchers quietly played the sounds for half of the pictures, too softly to wake anyone up. After the nap, people remembered the locations of those pictures better than the locations of the others.

Think about what each explanation predicts here. If sleep only keeps out new information, then every picture should be protected equally. The sounds shouldn't matter. But they did matter, and only for the pictures they belonged to. That's very hard to explain unless the sleeping brain is actively working on particular memories.

So I'd say the evidence supports the second explanation. That doesn't mean interference counts for nothing. Being awake and busy probably does weaken memories a little. It just can't be the whole story.

Finally, think about the night before a big test, when some of you stay up late studying until two or three in the morning. The common advice your parents gave you about sleep is right. And now you know what your brain would have been doing with those hours.

transcript:
OK, let's get going. Today's question sounds simple. How do ecologists know how many animals live in a place? A lot of people picture a scientist walking around with a clipboard, counting every single animal, one by one. That picture is almost always wrong. For most wild animals, nobody counts them all, because nobody could.

Take the garden snails in the flower beds behind this building. They hide under leaves and stones during the day, they come out mostly at night, and one snail looks a lot like the next. If you tried to count them all, you'd count some twice and miss most of the rest. So instead of counting, ecologists estimate, and one of the oldest ways to do that is called mark and recapture.

Here's how it works. On the first night, you collect, say, forty snails. You put a small dot of white paint on each shell, and you let them go exactly where you found them. Then you wait about a week, so the marked snails have time to mix back in with the others. On the second night you collect again. Let's say this time you find fifty snails, and ten of them have a dot. So one in five of your second catch is marked. If that's true of the whole garden, then your forty marked snails are about one fifth of all the snails, and the garden holds roughly two hundred. Notice how it goes. The fewer marked snails you find the second time, the bigger your estimate gets.

Now, that math only works if a few things are true, and this is where the method runs into its limits. First, the marks have to stay on. If heavy rain wears some of the paint off, you'll find fewer marked snails in the second catch than you really should.

Second, nothing should arrive or leave between the two nights. Snails are slow, so you might think that's easy. But over a week, young snails can hatch, some snails wander off into the next garden, and others get eaten. Song thrushes, for example, are birds that crack snail shells open on stones. A thrush that finds your flower bed can take quite a few snails before your second count.

Third, every snail should be equally easy to catch the second time. If the snails you handled learn to hide deeper, or if you always pick up the ones sitting in the open, your sample isn't fair.

Textbooks usually show this method as one neat line of math, and I think that's a bit misleading. The math is the easy part. The hard part is knowing whether those three conditions held in your garden that week.

So, is mark and recapture reliable for snails? Honestly, that's still an open question. In some experiments, researchers put a known number of snails into a fenced plot and then estimated it. Sometimes the estimate came close. Other times it was off by a third or more, and nobody's fully sure which of the problems caused it. I'm not saying throw the method out. I'm saying treat the number as a careful guess. Next week we'll try it ourselves and see how close we get.

transcript:
So today I want to talk about something that's sitting in almost every kitchen cupboard: food sealed in a can or a jar. Most people assume this was invented in a laboratory, that scientists first worked out what makes food go bad and then designed a way to stop it. It's a nice, tidy story. It's also backwards, and the way it really happened tells us something about how discoveries get made.

Let's go back to France in the seventeen nineties. The country was at war, and its soldiers and sailors had a serious problem. Fresh food rotted long before it could be eaten. Salted meat and hard biscuits lasted, but people got sick living on them for months. So the government offered a large cash prize to anyone who could find a better way to keep food.

The person who solved it wasn't a scientist at all. His name was Nicolas Appert, and he was a sweet maker in Paris, someone who spent his days boiling sugar and fruit. Appert had no theory. What he had was patience. He packed food into thick glass bottles, the heavy kind used for wine, pushed the corks in tight, sealed them with wax, and then set the bottles in boiling water. Then he waited, opened them weeks or months later, and wrote down what he found.

Here's the interesting part. He kept this up for roughly fifteen years. Peas needed one heating time, meat needed another, fruit another. If he heated a bottle too briefly, the food spoiled. If a cork let in even a little air, the food spoiled. Bit by bit, food by food, he built up a set of rules that worked, without ever knowing why they worked. Around eighteen ten he won the prize, and part of the deal was that he had to publish everything in a book, so anyone could copy his method.

So did the scientists step in at this point and explain it? Some tried. One of the leading chemists in France examined the bottles and announced that the answer was air. Keep the air out, he said, and food can't decay. It sounded convincing, and for a long time nobody could show otherwise.

It was wrong. About fifty years later, Louis Pasteur showed that food spoils because of microbes, living things far too small to see, which drift through the air and multiply in food. Appert's boiling killed the microbes already inside the bottle, and his tight seal stopped new ones from getting in. Air on its own, without the microbes, didn't make the food rot. So the explanation came half a century after the method, and the first scientific explanation pointed at the wrong thing.

So when someone tells you that understanding always comes first and useful inventions follow, I'd say be careful. Appert didn't need the theory. He needed careful notes and the stubbornness to open bottle after bottle of spoiled peas. Honestly, I find that more impressive than a lucky flash of insight, because there was no flash. There were just years of small tests.

For next class, think of one other everyday thing that people used successfully long before anyone could explain it.

transcript:
So today we're going to follow a piece of coastline through a very slow change. You've probably seen pictures of tall columns of rock standing in the sea, a little way out from a cliff. Geologists call these sea stacks, and I want to walk you through how one forms, step by step, because it doesn't happen all at once.

It starts with a headland. That's a piece of land that sticks out into the sea, with water on three sides. Because it sticks out, waves hit it from more than one direction, so it takes more of a beating than the bays on either side. Now, no rock is perfectly solid. Even hard rock has cracks running through it, and the cracks are where the sea gets to work.

Here's the first step. When a wave slams into a crack, it traps the air inside and squeezes it. Think of pushing down on a bicycle pump with your finger over the end. You can feel the air pushing back. In the rock, that squeezed air presses outward on the walls of the crack. Then the wave pulls back, the air suddenly expands, and the rock around it is shaken loose a little. Repeat that thousands of times a day, and a crack slowly becomes a gap. At the same time, waves throw sand and pebbles against the cliff, which grinds it away like sandpaper.

Step two. Over many years, the gaps widen into caves. And because the headland is hit from both sides, you often get a cave on each side, growing toward each other. When they finally meet in the middle, you've got an arch, a bridge of rock with the sea running underneath.

Step three. The arch doesn't last. Waves keep cutting at its base, while rain, wind and frost attack the top. Eventually the roof of the arch gets too thin to hold its own weight, and it falls. That's usually sudden, often during a storm. What's left standing on the seaward side, cut off from the land, is the stack.

And the story keeps going. The waves now attack the stack from every side, mostly at the bottom, where they hit hardest. It gets thinner at the base until one day it topples too. What remains is a short stump, which may only show at low tide.

How do we know the stages really come in this order? I'm confident they do, and here's why. First, along one coast you can often see every stage side by side: a headland with caves, an arch further along, then stacks and stumps. Second, we have old photographs. At a place called Harrock, a photograph from about a hundred years ago shows an arch. Today, in that same spot, there's no arch, just a single stack standing alone in the water.

So next time you see a sea stack, remember that you're looking at what's left of a headland, and that the next stage has already begun.

OK, let's get started. Today I want to look at how the centre of a town can move over time, and I'm going to use one small example, the town of Jastow. You'll see this pattern in lots of places, but a small town makes it easier to follow.

Jastow began as a settlement beside a ford. A ford is a shallow place in a river where people and carts can cross. For roughly two hundred years, everything important in Jastow stood within a few minutes' walk of that crossing. The market square, the inn, the blacksmith and most of the houses were all right there.

Then things started to change. In eighteen sixty-four a stone bridge was built a little way upstream, and in eighteen eighty-five a railway station opened on the hill north of the town. By nineteen hundred, the busiest street in Jastow was the new high street running up to the station, and the old market square by the river was mostly warehouses.

So the obvious question is why. Why did a whole town centre climb a hill?

One explanation points to the railway. Goods and visitors now arrived at the top of the hill, so shops followed them. Think about it from a shopkeeper's point of view. You want to be where the people are. And there's good evidence for this. Business records show that three of the town's biggest stores moved up to the high street within ten years of the station opening.

But here's the interesting part. A second explanation points to the river itself. A set of old letters describes floods in the low streets in eighteen fifty-two and again in eighteen fifty-nine, years before the station existed. And a map drawn in eighteen seventy already shows new houses going up on higher ground. So some families may have been leaving the riverside before the trains came at all.

Now, which explanation is right? Honestly, we don't know yet, and both have weak spots. Let's start with the floods. All of those letters were written by members of one family, so we can't tell whether the water reached the whole lower town or just their street. And the new houses on the map might simply show Jastow growing, not people escaping the river.

The railway story has a problem too. Jastow's market licence, that's the document that gave the town the right to hold a weekly market, wasn't moved to the high street until nineteen ten. That's twenty-five years after the station opened. If the railway pulled everything uphill, why did the market stay down by the river for so long?

So historians are still arguing about it. Right now a local group is going through old tax records, which list who lived at each address every ten years. Those might finally settle it, or they might just raise new questions.

For Thursday, please look at the two maps in your packet, one from eighteen fifty and one from nineteen hundred, and write down three changes you notice between them.

transcript:
Today we're going to take one decision and follow everything that came after it. About two hundred years ago, the river town of Lindmere had a terrible winter. The river froze early, the boats that usually brought firewood down from the hills couldn't get through, and the price of a bundle of wood more than doubled in a month. Poor families were burning their own chairs to stay warm.

So the town council did something that sounded kind. It passed a rule that no one in Lindmere could sell a bundle of firewood for more than four pennies, which was roughly the price before the river froze. The thinking was simple. If wood stays cheap, everyone can afford to heat their homes. I'm going to argue that this rule did more harm than good, and I want to show you why by following its effects one at a time.

The first effect came within a week. The sellers who brought wood into town by cart, over the hill road, found that the trip wasn't worth it anymore. The road was icy, the horses had to be fed, and at four pennies a bundle they lost money on every load. So most of them simply turned around and sold their wood in Mardale, the next town along, where there was no limit. Lindmere didn't get cheap wood. It got less wood.

The second effect was about quality. The sellers who did stay found other ways to protect themselves. Bundles got smaller. Then they got wetter. Sellers mixed in green wood, which means wood that's freshly cut. It smokes badly and gives off much less heat. Officially, the price was still four pennies, but a family now needed two of those bundles to get the warmth that one used to give.

The third effect is the one I find most troubling. There wasn't enough wood for everyone, so sellers had to decide who got it, and they didn't decide by need. They sold to their regular customers, to friends, to anyone who could offer something extra on the side, a sack of flour, say, or a favour. The families with nothing extra to offer, the very families the rule was written for, ended up at the back of the line.

Here's the interesting part. A town record from that February lists how many carts came in over the hill road each week. Before the rule, it was around thirty. Three weeks after it, only nine carts came in, far fewer than before. Then in March the council quietly dropped the limit, and within two weeks the number was back above twenty. Prices were high, yes, but there was wood to buy.

So was the council wrong to want to help? No. The goal was a good one. My point is that the tool didn't fit the goal. If the council had used the town's money to buy wood and hand it to the poorest families, the sellers would have kept coming, and the help would have gone where it was needed.

For Thursday, write one paragraph on this question. Who, if anyone, gained from the rule?

OK, so last week we looked at how people painted animals on cave walls thousands of years ago. Today I want to talk about a problem those paintings face in our own time, and about one solution that was tried.

Picture this. In nineteen forty, a few teenagers exploring the hills in France found a narrow opening in the ground. They climbed down, and the walls inside were covered with paintings of horses, deer and huge wild cattle, in reds, yellows and blacks. The paintings were roughly seventeen thousand years old, and they were in amazing condition. Why? Because for all that time, the cave had been sealed. The air inside barely moved. The temperature stayed almost the same, all year round.

A few years later, the cave was opened to visitors, and it became hugely popular. By the nineteen fifties, more than a thousand people a day were walking through it. Now, here's the problem. Every visitor breathes out warm, wet air. Bring in a thousand people a day, and the air in a small cave changes completely. It gets warmer, and the walls get damp. Visitors also carried in tiny living things on their shoes and clothes. Before long, green patches of algae, which are simple plant-like growths, started spreading across the rock. The very people who'd come to admire the paintings were slowly harming them.

So what was the solution? In nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public. Completely. About twenty years later, a copy was opened nearby. Artists spent years recreating the most famous walls with the same kinds of colors, so visitors could see something close to the real thing without breathing on it.

Did it work? This is where it gets complicated. Closing the cave stopped the crowds, and the algae was brought under control. But around the year two thousand, a white fungus suddenly spread across the floor and walls, decades after the visitors had gone. Then black spots appeared. Scientists still argue about why. Some point to a new air-control system that had just been put in. Others blame the chemicals used to kill the fungus, which may have fed the next outbreak. Honestly, nobody's sure, and every treatment seems to change the cave in a new way.

The copy raises its own question, too. And I have to say, the copy is better than I expected. I've seen photos of a real wall and the copied wall side by side, and I couldn't tell them apart, not even the colors. Still, there's an argument that the point of a place like that is standing where the painters actually stood, and no copy can give you that. The other argument is that if the choice is between a copy and losing the paintings forever, the copy wins easily.

So I can't give you a neat ending today. Closing the cave clearly helped with the first problem. Whether it's enough to save the paintings in the long run, we just don't know yet. For next class, write half a page on this question. If a painted cave were found near here tomorrow, would you open it to visitors or not, and why?

transcript:
Okay, let's get started. Today's topic is something a lot of you probably have in your bag right now: noise-cancelling headphones. If you believe the advertisements, you put them on, press a button, and the whole world goes silent. Planes, traffic, people talking, all of it, gone. I want to show you why that picture is wrong, and why these headphones work brilliantly on some sounds and much less well on others.

First, a little science. Sound is a wave of pressure moving through the air. The air gets squeezed a little, then stretched a little, over and over. Now, imagine two waves on the surface of a pond. If the high point of one wave meets the low point of another, they flatten each other out. Scientists call this destructive interference, which just means two waves cancelling each other.

Noise-cancelling headphones use exactly that trick. There are tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup. They listen to the noise around you, and a small chip inside works out the opposite wave, a kind of mirror image, and plays it through the speaker along with your music. Where the noise pushes, the headphones pull. In the best case, the two cancel, and your ear hears much less.

Here's the interesting part. Let's compare two cases. Case one, you're on a long flight, and the engines make a deep, steady hum. A low sound like that has long, slow waves, and it hardly changes from one second to the next. So the chip has an easy job. It can predict what's coming, and even if it's a tiny fraction of a second late, a long wave hasn't moved much in that time. The result is impressive. Most of that hum seems to just disappear.

Case two, you're in the school cafeteria. Someone is talking at the next table, a tray crashes to the floor, a friend laughs. These sounds are higher, and they start and stop suddenly. Higher sounds have short, quick waves. Now that same tiny delay matters a lot, because by the time the opposite wave arrives, a short wave has already changed. The chip simply can't keep up. For sounds like these, most of the work is done by something much older, the soft cushions around your ears. They block sound the same way covering your ears with your hands does, and they're actually better at blocking high sounds than low ones.

Ask anyone who flies a lot, and they'll tell you the same thing. These headphones are wonderful against engine noise, but you can still hear the person in the next seat talking. That's a common belief, and the science says it's correct. Even very good headphones still let a lot of a voice through.

So, no, noise-cancelling headphones don't erase the world. They're excellent at one kind of sound, the low and steady kind, and fairly ordinary at the rest. If you were planning to buy a pair to study in a noisy cafeteria, you might be disappointed. If you want a quieter bus ride, though, they're worth it. For Thursday, I'd like you to list five sounds you hear on your way to school and decide which of the two cases each one belongs to.

OK, let's get started. Today I want to show you an experiment that's simple enough to do in a school gym, and the result still surprises me every time I teach it.

In a typical study, a group of volunteers trains only one arm, the right one. Three times a week, for about six weeks, they squeeze a hand grip or lift a small weight with the right hand. The left hand does nothing special. It just rests on the table. At the end, the researchers test the strength of both hands.

The right hand is stronger, of course. That's not the interesting part. Here's the interesting part. The left hand, which never trained at all, is stronger too. Not by as much. In most studies the untrained side gains roughly half of what the trained side gains, and sometimes less. But it's a real gain, and it shows up again and again. Scientists call this cross education, because the training seems to cross over from one side of the body to the other. It was first described more than a hundred years ago, and it's been tested many times since.

So how can a muscle get stronger without being used? Here's the first clue. When researchers measure the muscles of the untrained arm, they haven't grown. They're the same size as before. So the change can't be in the muscle itself. It's in the nervous system, in the brain and the nerves that tell muscles what to do.

Think of it this way. A muscle is made of many thin fibers, and your brain has to switch them on. When a movement is new, the brain switches on only some of them, and not quite at the same moment. With practice, it gets better at sending the signal, so more fibers join in, with better timing. The two halves of the brain are closely connected and share a lot of information, so some of that learning seems to reach the control of the other arm as well. You could say the left side picks up the lesson without doing the homework.

Now, why does this matter outside a laboratory? Imagine you break your left wrist, and it spends a few weeks in a cast. Muscles that aren't used get weaker, and quickly. In several studies, volunteers had one arm held still in a cast for a few weeks, and some of them trained their free arm. When the cast came off, those who had trained had lost much less strength in the arm inside it than those who didn't train at all. Working the free arm helped protect the one in the cast. No machines, nothing expensive, and some physical therapists already build it into their plans.

One last thing to think about. When people first start lifting weights, they often get noticeably stronger within two or three weeks, long before their muscles look any different. Keep that in mind for next time, when we look at how muscles actually grow.
